title: Report 1: residuals against everything
body: A residuals-vs-fitted plot can look fine while a residuals-vs-predictor plot does not. Plot your residuals against every column in the codebook, including the ones that are not in your model, and add a smooth curve (geom_smooth()).
A bend says the form of a predictor is wrong. A trend in a predictor you left out says it belongs in the model. A flat cloud says that column has nothing more to tell you.

Every column includes state_id. Make boxplots of your residuals by state. If some states sit mostly above zero and others mostly below, your model is missing something that every county in a state shares.

title: Report 2: when a straight line is not enough
body: If a residual plot from Report 1 bends, a spline in that predictor is one line of code: splines::ns(x, df = 3) inside lm(). It is still a linear model.
Before you keep it, ask whether the bend is real: compare the models with a nested F-test (anova(smaller, bigger)), and check that the training improvement survives on the leaderboard.

title: Report 3: are your intervals the same width everywhere?
body: Look at your intervals on the log scale. Are they all the same width? Should they be?

Plot the absolute residuals (or log squared residuals) against your fitted values and against every column in the codebook, including the ones that are not in your model. If the spread changes systematically, your intervals are too wide in some counties and too narrow in others, and the interval score charges you for both.
A quick check: compute your coverage separately for the counties below and above the median of whatever variable the spread tracks. Honest intervals cover about 90% in both groups.
